notes.b: Pastries are grouped by how the fat is combined with the flour and how the pastry rises, and this decides the texture of the finished pastry. Knowing the groups lets you name a type, say how it differs from another, and match each to a dish.
points: Short pastries (shortcrust, sweet shortcrust, rich shortcrust, biscuit and cheese pastry): the fat is rubbed into the flour so that it coats the flour particles and limits gluten (the stretchy protein in flour), giving a crumbly texture.
Flaked or laminated pastries (rough puff, flaky and puff): pieces or layers of fat are folded into the dough, so layers of dough and fat separate and rise, giving a flaky texture.
Choux pastry: a cooked paste of water, fat and flour, with beaten egg added. It contains no rubbed-in fat and is raised by steam into a hollow shell, which is why it suits eclairs and profiteroles.
Filo pastry: very thin sheets of dough layered with fat or oil, which become crisp when baked, as in samosas and strudel.
Suet pastry is a type of its own: the fat is shredded suet, not rubbed in, and it is made with self-raising flour then steamed or baked, as in a steamed pudding. It can also be boiled.

Matching dishes: shortcrust for apple tart, quiche and (as rich shortcrust) mince pies; rough puff or puff for sausage rolls, vol-au-vents and pie toppings; choux for eclairs and profiteroles; filo for samosas and strudel; suet for steamed pudding.

Two types differ in their ingredients, proportions, method, characteristics or appearance. For example, shortcrust has the fat rubbed in while rough puff has the fat left in pieces and folded in, and rough puff uses a higher proportion of fat.
notes.tip: If asked to name two types of pastry and a different dish from each, pick two clearly different types, such as shortcrust with apple tart and choux with eclairs. If asked for one difference, state one of ingredients, proportions, method, characteristics or appearance.

notes.b: Shortcrust is the most common short pastry and forms the base for sweet and savoury tarts and pies. Rubbing the fat into the flour coats the flour with fat, which limits gluten and makes the pastry short, meaning crumbly.
points: Ingredients: plain flour, a pinch of salt, cold fat (butter, margarine or lard, or a mix) in roughly half the weight of the flour, and cold water to bind; sugar is added for sweet shortcrust.
Step 1: sift the flour and salt into a bowl, which aerates the flour (puts air into it) and removes lumps.

Step 2: rub the cold fat into the flour with the fingertips, lifting the mixture to add air, until it resembles fine breadcrumbs. Cold fingertips keep the fat from melting, and the fat coating the flour is what limits gluten.
Step 3: add cold water gradually, mixing with a round-bladed knife until the dough just comes together. Too much liquid makes the pastry tough.
Step 4: bring the dough together lightly, wrap and chill it so the gluten relaxes and the fat firms. Heavy handling would develop the gluten and toughen the pastry.
Step 5: roll lightly on a floured surface, line the tin, and chill again before baking so the pastry does not shrink.

Step 6: bake in a preheated hot oven (about 200 degrees Celsius, gas 6) until golden, then reduce the heat if the pastry is browning too quickly. Blind bake a case (bake it empty) when the filling is not cooked, such as quiche, to prevent a soggy base.

Presentation: sweet shortcrust is dusted with icing sugar or glazed with beaten egg or milk; savoury shortcrust is used for quiche and pies, with the edges crimped or fluted. Used for tarts, pies and mince pies, the pastry should be neat, evenly browned, crisp and not shrunk.
notes.tip: In a longer question on preparing one named pastry, give the ingredients, the method in order, how it is cooked and how it is presented. Say bring the dough together lightly, not knead, because kneading toughens shortcrust.

notes.b: Rough puff is a puff pastry in which the fat is left in pieces rather than rubbed in, and the dough is folded in several turns to create layers. It uses a high proportion of hard fat (about three-quarters of the weight of the flour), so it is richer and lighter than shortcrust.
points: Ingredients: plain flour, a pinch of salt, hard fat (butter or block margarine), and cold water to bind; a little lemon juice is optional.

Step 1: cut the cold fat into cubes or irregular pieces, leave them visible and mix them lightly with the flour, binding the dough with cold water. The lumps of fat must stay, because they make the layers later.
Step 2: roll the dough into a long rectangle, fold the bottom third up and the top third down, then turn the dough a quarter turn.
Step 3: repeat the roll, fold and turn several times, resting and chilling between turns so the fat stays firm and the layers stay distinct.
Step 4: roll to the required thickness and chill before cutting so that the edges stay sharp.
Step 5: bake in a very hot, preheated oven (about 220 degrees Celsius, gas 7 to 8) and do not open the door early.
Why it rises: the water in the dough and fat turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, then the fat melts into the dough and the layers set, so the pastry rises and becomes flaky and light.

Presentation: sausage rolls, vol-au-vents, pie lids and toppings, and Eccles cakes. Glaze with egg wash, keeping it off the cut edges so the layers can rise; the layers should be even and golden, with sharp edges.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the two methods: shortcrust is made by rubbing in, rough puff by folding and rolling. If asked why puff rises, answer steam lifting the layers of dough and fat, not a raising agent.

notes.b: Light, crisp pastry depends on keeping the fat solid, handling the dough as little as possible and not building up gluten. These guidelines apply to both types and explain why a pastry turns out tough, shrunk, soggy or heavy.
points: Keep the ingredients, hands, utensils and kitchen cool so that the fat does not melt before baking.
Weigh ingredients accurately so that the flour-to-fat ratio is correct.
Sieve the flour to introduce air, and rub in lightly with the fingertips.
Add cold liquid gradually; too much liquid makes the pastry sticky or tough and increases shrinkage.
Avoid overhandling: working the dough develops gluten, which makes pastry tough, so handle it as little as possible.
Rest and chill pastry before rolling and baking so that the gluten relaxes and the pastry does not shrink.
Roll lightly in one direction and evenly, and avoid stretching the dough, which causes shrinkage.
Bake in a preheated hot oven, on a hot baking tray, and use blind baking for fillings that are not baked, such as quiche, which keeps the base crisp.
notes.tip: Questions ask for about three guidelines for light, successful pastry: choose three such as cool ingredients, accurate weighing and resting, and add the reason for each. If asked why pastry is tough, shrunk, soggy or heavy, think overhandling, too much water, no resting or an oven that is too cool.

keyTerms.definition: A short pastry made by rubbing cold fat into flour and binding with cold water, giving a crumbly texture.
A puff pastry in which pieces of fat are folded into the dough in several turns to form flaky layers.
A cooked paste of water, fat and flour, mixed with beaten egg, that rises by steam into a hollow shell.
A pastry made from very thin sheets of dough layered with fat or oil, which become crisp when baked.
A pastry made with shredded suet and self-raising flour, which is steamed or boiled.
Working cold fat into flour with the fingertips until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs.
Baking a pastry case before its filling is added, usually with baking beans or paper to keep its shape.
The contraction of pastry during baking, caused by overstretched gluten or insufficient resting.

questions.prompt: Name three guidelines that help a student make a light shortcrust pastry, and explain why each one helps.
questions.model: Keep ingredients and utensils cool, so the fat does not melt and the pastry stays short. Handle the dough as little as possible, because overhandling develops gluten and makes the pastry tough. Add cold water gradually, so the dough is bound without becoming sticky or tough. Other acceptable guidelines include chilling before rolling, rolling lightly and using a preheated hot oven.

questions.prompt: Describe the preparation, cooking and presentation of rough puff pastry, and explain the principles a cook must follow for the pastry to rise evenly and become flaky.
questions.model: Preparation: cold fat is cut into pieces and mixed with flour and salt, then bound with cold water to form a dough. Folding: the dough is rolled into a rectangle, folded in three and turned a quarter turn, then this is repeated several times with chilling between turns, so that layers of dough and fat form. Cooking: the pastry is baked in a very hot preheated oven; the water in the fat turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, so the pastry rises and becomes flaky. Presentation: it is cut to size, with sharp edges, and used for sausage rolls, vol-au-vents or pie toppings, with even, golden layers. Principles: keep the fat cool so it stays in pieces; do not overhandle the dough; chill between turns and before cutting; roll evenly and avoid stretching; use a hot oven and do not let the fat melt before baking.
